claim: Eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 (eIF3) is a central player in recruitment of the pre-initiation complex (PIC) to mRNA.
source: Eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 (eIF3) is a central player in recruitment of the pre-initiation complex (PIC) to mRNA.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract summarizing the established role of eIF3, supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations throughout eIF3 disrupt its interaction with the PIC.
source: Mutations throughout eIF3 disrupt its interaction with the PIC and diminish its ability to accelerate recruitment to a native yeast mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing binding affinities of eIF3 variants.

claim: Mutations throughout eIF3 diminish its ability to accelerate recruitment to a native yeast mRNA.
source: Mutations throughout eIF3 disrupt its interaction with the PIC and diminish its ability to accelerate recruitment to a native yeast mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data on mRNA recruitment presented in the manuscript.

claim: Alterations to the eIF3a CTD significantly slow mRNA recruitment.
source: Alterations to the eIF3a CTD and eIF3b/i/g significantly slow mRNA recruitment, and mutations within eIF3b/i/g destabilize eIF2•GTP•Met-tRNAi binding to the PIC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing recruitment kinetics with eIF3a CTD mutants.

claim: Alterations to eIF3b/i/g significantly slow mRNA recruitment.
source: Alterations to the eIF3a CTD and eIF3b/i/g significantly slow mRNA recruitment, and mutations within eIF3b/i/g destabilize eIF2•GTP•Met-tRNAi binding to the PIC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing recruitment kinetics with eIF3b/i/g mutants.

claim: Mutations within eIF3b/i/g destabilize eIF2•GTP•Met-tRNAi binding to the PIC.
source: Alterations to the eIF3a CTD and eIF3b/i/g significantly slow mRNA recruitment, and mutations within eIF3b/i/g destabilize eIF2•GTP•Met-tRNAi binding to the PIC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data measuring TC binding affinity in the presence of eIF3 variants.

claim: eIF3 has a critical role in stabilizing mRNA interactions at the exit channel that requires the eIF3a NTD.
source: Using model mRNAs lacking contacts with the 40S entry or exit channels, we uncovered a critical role for eIF3 requiring the eIF3a NTD, in stabilizing mRNA interactions at the exit channel, and an ancillary role at the entry channel requiring residues of the eIF3a CTD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using model mRNAs with different AUG positions.

claim: eIF3 has an ancillary role at the entry channel requiring residues of the eIF3a CTD.
source: Using model mRNAs lacking contacts with the 40S entry or exit channels, we uncovered a critical role for eIF3 requiring the eIF3a NTD, in stabilizing mRNA interactions at the exit channel, and an ancillary role at the entry channel requiring residues of the eIF3a CTD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using model mRNAs with different AUG positions.

claim: Defects at each channel can be rescued by filling the other channel with mRNA.
source: These functions are redundant: defects at each channel can be rescued by filling the other channel with mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of recruitment defects with mRNAs of varying lengths.

claim: Translation initiation in eukaryotes requires the participation of 12 initiation factors (eIFs).
source: To ensure faithful identification of the start codon, translation initiation in eukaryotes follows a complex, multi-step pathway which requires the participation of 12 initiation factors (eIFs) (reviewed in: (Aitken and Lorsch, 2012; Hinnebusch, 2014; Jackson et al., 2010; Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Valásek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles summarizing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The process of translation initiation begins with the formation of a 43S pre-initiation complex (PIC).
source: The process begins with the formation of a 43S pre-initiation complex (PIC), in which the initiator methionyl tRNA (Met-tRNAi) is initially positioned as a tRNAi•eIF2•GTP ternary complex (TC) on the small (40S) ribosomal subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the translation initiation pathway.

claim: The 43S PIC contains eIF1 and eIF1A bound near the 40S P and A sites, respectively.
source: The 43S PIC further contains eIF1 and eIF1A bound, respectively, near the 40S P and A sites, as well as eIF5 and eIF3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition and structure of the 43S PIC.

claim: GTP hydrolysis by eIF2 can proceed within the PIC, but the release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) is blocked by the presence of eIF1.
source: GTP hydrolysis by eIF2 can proceed within the PIC, but the release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) is blocked by the presence of eIF1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the regulation of GTP hydrolysis during translation initiation.

claim: The PIC is loaded onto the 5' end of the mRNA with the collaboration of eIF4B and the eIF4F complex.
source: With the collaboration of eIF4B and the eIF4F complex composed of eIF4A, eIF4G, and eIF4E, the PIC is then loaded onto the 5' end of the mRNA, from which it scans in the 3' direction to locate the AUG codon, thus generating the 48S PIC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of eIF4 factors in mRNA recruitment.

claim: The PIC scans in the 3' direction to locate the AUG codon.
source: With the collaboration of eIF4B and the eIF4F complex composed of eIF4A, eIF4G, and eIF4E, the PIC is then loaded onto the 5' end of the mRNA, from which it scans in the 3' direction to locate the AUG codon, thus generating the 48S PIC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the scanning mechanism during translation initiation.

claim: Loading onto the mRNA and subsequent scanning are facilitated by an open conformation of the PIC enforced by the binding of eIF1.
source: Both loading onto the mRNA and subsequent scanning are facilitated by an open conformation of the PIC enforced by the binding of eIF1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of eIF1 in maintaining PIC conformation.

claim: Recognition of the AUG codon triggers eviction of eIF1.
source: Recognition of the AUG codon triggers eviction of eIF1, gating Pi release by eIF2 and provoking a transition from the open PIC conformation to a closed conformation that arrests scanning.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of start codon recognition.

claim: Recognition of the AUG codon gates Pi release by eIF2.
source: Recognition of the AUG codon triggers eviction of eIF1, gating Pi release by eIF2 and provoking a transition from the open PIC conformation to a closed conformation that arrests scanning.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of start codon recognition.

claim: Recognition of the AUG codon provokes a transition from the open PIC conformation to a closed conformation that arrests scanning.
source: Recognition of the AUG codon triggers eviction of eIF1, gating Pi release by eIF2 and provoking a transition from the open PIC conformation to a closed conformation that arrests scanning.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of start codon recognition.

claim: Joining of a 60S ribosomal subunit completes assembly of the 80S initiation complex.
source: Joining of a 60S ribosomal subunit completes assembly of the 80S initiation complex, which can then proceed to the elongation cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the final step of translation initiation.

claim: eIF3 is the largest of the initiation factors.
source: The largest of the initiation factors is eIF3, a multisubunit complex that binds the 40S subunit and has been implicated in events throughout the initiation pathway (Hinnebusch, 2006, 2011; Valásek, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: eIF3 is a multisubunit complex that binds the 40S subunit.
source: The largest of the initiation factors is eIF3, a multisubunit complex that binds the 40S subunit and has been implicated in events throughout the initiation pathway (Hinnebusch, 2006, 2011; Valásek, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: eIF3 has been implicated in events throughout the initiation pathway.
source: The largest of the initiation factors is eIF3, a multisubunit complex that binds the 40S subunit and has been implicated in events throughout the initiation pathway (Hinnebusch, 2006, 2011; Valásek, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In humans, eIF3 is composed of 13 individual subunits.
source: In humans, eIF3 is composed of 13 individual subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of human eIF3.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, eIF3 comprises 5 essential subunits: eIF3a, eIF3b, eIF3c, eIF3i, and eIF3g.
source: In the yeast S. cerevisiae, eIF3 comprises 5 essential subunits thought to represent a core complex capable of performing the essential tasks of eIF3: eIF3a, eIF3b, eIF3c, eIF3i, and eIF3g.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of yeast eIF3.

claim: A sixth nonessential and nonstoichiometric subunit, eIF3j, associates loosely with the eIF3 complex.
source: A sixth nonessential and nonstoichiometric subunit, eIF3j, associates loosely with the complex (Elantak et al., 2010; Fraser et al., 2004; Nielsen et al., 2006; Valasek et al., 2001a), though its role during initiation remains unclear (Beznosková et al., 2013; Fraser et al., 2007; Mitchell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The role of eIF3j during initiation remains unclear.
source: A sixth nonessential and nonstoichiometric subunit, eIF3j, associates loosely with the complex (Elantak et al., 2010; Fraser et al., 2004; Nielsen et al., 2006; Valasek et al., 2001a), though its role during initiation remains unclear (Beznosková et al., 2013; Fraser et al., 2007; Mitchell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating ongoing uncertainty about eIF3j function.

claim: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes the 43S PIC.
source: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes both the 43S (Asano et al., 2000; Kolupaeva et al., 2005; Maag et al., 2005; Valášek et al., 2003) and 48S PIC (Chiu et al., 2010; Khoshnevis et al., 2014; Phan et al., 2001) and interacts with TC (Valášek et al., 2002), eIF1 (Fletcher et al., 1999; Valasek et al., 2004), eIF1A (Olsen et al., 2003), and eIF5 (Asano et al., 2001; Phan et al., 1998), as well as with the 40S subunit near both the mRNA entry and exit channels (Kouba et al., 2012a, 2012b; Pisarev et al., 2008; Valášek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes the 48S PIC.
source: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes both the 43S (Asano et al., 2000; Kolupaeva et al., 2005; Maag et al., 2005; Valášek et al., 2003) and 48S PIC (Chiu et al., 2010; Khoshnevis et al., 2014; Phan et al., 2001) and interacts with TC (Valášek et al., 2002), eIF1 (Fletcher et al., 1999; Valasek et al., 2004), eIF1A (Olsen et al., 2003), and eIF5 (Asano et al., 2001; Phan et al., 1998), as well as with the 40S subunit near both the mRNA entry and exit channels (Kouba et al., 2012a, 2012b; Pisarev et al., 2008; Valášek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: eIF3 interacts with TC.
source: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes both the 43S (Asano et al., 2000; Kolupaeva et al., 2005; Maag et al., 2005; Valášek et al., 2003) and 48S PIC (Chiu et al., 2010; Khoshnevis et al., 2014; Phan et al., 2001) and interacts with TC (Valášek et al., 2002), eIF1 (Fletcher et al., 1999; Valasek et al., 2004), eIF1A (Olsen et al., 2003), and eIF5 (Asano et al., 2001; Phan et al., 1998), as well as with the 40S subunit near both the mRNA entry and exit channels (Kouba et al., 2012a, 2012b; Pisarev et al., 2008; Valášek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valášek et al., 2002.

claim: eIF3 interacts with eIF1.
source: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes both the 43S (Asano et al., 2000; Kolupaeva et al., 2005; Maag et al., 2005; Valášek et al., 2003) and 48S PIC (Chiu et al., 2010; Khoshnevis et al., 2014; Phan et al., 2001) and interacts with TC (Valášek et al., 2002), eIF1 (Fletcher et al., 1999; Valasek et al., 2004), eIF1A (Olsen et al., 2003), and eIF5 (Asano et al., 2001; Phan et al., 1998), as well as with the 40S subunit near both the mRNA entry and exit channels (Kouba et al., 2012a, 2012b; Pisarev et al., 2008; Valášek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fletcher et al., 1999 and Valasek et al., 2004.

claim: eIF3 interacts with eIF1A.
source: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes both the 43S (Asano et al., 2000; Kolupaeva et al., 2005; Maag et al., 2005; Valášek et al., 2003) and 48S PIC (Chiu et al., 2010; Khoshnevis et al., 2014; Phan et al., 2001) and interacts with TC (Valášek et al., 2002), eIF1 (Fletcher et al., 1999; Valasek et al., 2004), eIF1A (Olsen et al., 2003), and eIF5 (Asano et al., 2001; Phan et al., 1998), as well as with the 40S subunit near both the mRNA entry and exit channels (Kouba et al., 2012a, 2012b; Pisarev et al., 2008; Valášek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2003.

claim: eIF3 interacts with eIF5.
source: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes both the 43S (Asano et al., 2000; Kolupaeva et al., 2005; Maag et al., 2005; Valášek et al., 2003) and 48S PIC (Chiu et al., 2010; Khoshnevis et al., 2014; Phan et al., 2001) and interacts with TC (Valášek et al., 2002), eIF1 (Fletcher et al., 1999; Valasek et al., 2004), eIF1A (Olsen et al., 2003), and eIF5 (Asano et al., 2001; Phan et al., 1998), as well as with the 40S subunit near both the mRNA entry and exit channels (Kouba et al., 2012a, 2012b; Pisarev et al., 2008; Valášek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asano et al., 2001 and Phan et al., 1998.

claim: eIF3 interacts with the 40S subunit near both the mRNA entry and exit channels.
source: Genetic and biochemical evidence indicate that eIF3 stabilizes both the 43S (Asano et al., 2000; Kolupaeva et al., 2005; Maag et al., 2005; Valášek et al., 2003) and 48S PIC (Chiu et al., 2010; Khoshnevis et al., 2014; Phan et al., 2001) and interacts with TC (Valášek et al., 2002), eIF1 (Fletcher et al., 1999; Valasek et al., 2004), eIF1A (Olsen et al., 2003), and eIF5 (Asano et al., 2001; Phan et al., 1998), as well as with the 40S subunit near both the mRNA entry and exit channels (Kouba et al., 2012a, 2012b; Pisarev et al., 2008; Valášek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kouba et al., 2012a, 2012b; Pisarev et al., 2008; Valášek et al., 2003.

claim: eIF3 plays roles in loading the mRNA onto the PIC.
source: eIF3 also plays roles in loading the mRNA onto the PIC (Jivotovskaya et al., 2006; Mitchell et al., 2010; Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002) and in scanning of the mRNA to locate the start codon (Chiu et al., 2010; Cuchalova et al., 2010; Karásková et al., 2012; Nielsen et al., 2006; Valasek et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: eIF3 plays roles in scanning of the mRNA to locate the start codon.
source: eIF3 also plays roles in loading the mRNA onto the PIC (Jivotovskaya et al., 2006; Mitchell et al., 2010; Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002) and in scanning of the mRNA to locate the start codon (Chiu et al., 2010; Cuchalova et al., 2010; Karásková et al., 2012; Nielsen et al., 2006; Valasek et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The depletion of eIF3 from yeast cells sharply decreases the amount of mRNA associated with PICs in vivo.
source: The depletion of eIF3 from yeast cells sharply decreases the amount of mRNA associated with PICs in vivo (Jivotovskaya et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jivotovskaya et al., 2006.

claim: Yeast eIF3 is required for detectable recruitment of native mRNAs in the yeast reconstituted translation initiation system in vitro.
source: In vitro, yeast eIF3 is required for detectable recruitment of native mRNAs in the yeast reconstituted translation initiation system (Mitchell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2010.

claim: Mutations in the C-terminal domain (CTD) of eIF3a impair mRNA recruitment in yeast cells without affecting the integrity of the PIC.
source: Mutations in the C-terminal domain (CTD) of eIF3a, which interacts with the 40S subunit near the mRNA entry channel, impair mRNA recruitment in yeast cells without affecting the integrity of the PIC (Chiu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chiu et al., 2010.

claim: The eIF3a CTD interacts with the 40S subunit near the mRNA entry channel.
source: Mutations in the C-terminal domain (CTD) of eIF3a, which interacts with the 40S subunit near the mRNA entry channel, impair mRNA recruitment in yeast cells without affecting the integrity of the PIC (Chiu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chiu et al., 2010.

claim: The eIF3a N-terminal domain (NTD) interacts functionally with mRNA near the exit channel.
source: The eIF3a N-terminal domain (NTD) interacts functionally with mRNA near the exit channel, enhancing reinitiation upon translation of the upstream open reading frame 1 (uORF1) and uORF2 of GCN4 mRNA in a manner dependent on the sequence upstream of these two uORFs (Gunišová et al., 2016; Gunišová and Valášek, 2014; Munzarová et al., 2011; Szamecz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The eIF3a NTD enhances reinitiation upon translation of uORF1 and uORF2 of GCN4 mRNA in a manner dependent on the sequence upstream of these two uORFs.
source: The eIF3a N-terminal domain (NTD) interacts functionally with mRNA near the exit channel, enhancing reinitiation upon translation of the upstream open reading frame 1 (uORF1) and uORF2 of GCN4 mRNA in a manner dependent on the sequence upstream of these two uORFs (Gunišová et al., 2016; Gunišová and Valášek, 2014; Munzarová et al., 2011; Szamecz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mammalian eIF3 can be cross-linked to mRNA at positions 8–17 nucleotides upstream of the AUG codon.
source: Consistent with this, mammalian eIF3 can be cross-linked to mRNA at positions 8–17 nucleotides upstream of the AUG codon (Pisarev et al., 2008), near the exit channel, and a mutation within the eIF3a NTD, which has been located near the exit channel in structures of the PIC, interferes with mRNA recruitment in yeast cells (Khoshnevis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pisarev et al., 2008.

claim: A mutation within the eIF3a NTD interferes with mRNA recruitment in yeast cells.
source: Consistent with this, mammalian eIF3 can be cross-linked to mRNA at positions 8–17 nucleotides upstream of the AUG codon (Pisarev et al., 2008), near the exit channel, and a mutation within the eIF3a NTD, which has been located near the exit channel in structures of the PIC, interferes with mRNA recruitment in yeast cells (Khoshnevis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khoshnevis et al., 2014.

claim: The eIF3a NTD has been located near the exit channel in structures of the PIC.
source: Consistent with this, mammalian eIF3 can be cross-linked to mRNA at positions 8–17 nucleotides upstream of the AUG codon (Pisarev et al., 2008), near the exit channel, and a mutation within the eIF3a NTD, which has been located near the exit channel in structures of the PIC, interferes with mRNA recruitment in yeast cells (Khoshnevis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khoshnevis et al., 2014 and structural studies.

claim: In the py48S-closed structure, eIF3 is found bound primarily to the 40S solvent face, via two main points of contact.
source: In these structures, eIF3 (shown in blues and reds from py48S-closed structure) is found bound primarily to the 40S (light grey) solvent face, via two main points of contact.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1 and cited structural studies.

claim: The eIF3a NTD and eIF3c CTD PCI domains form a heterodimer that binds below the platform, near the mRNA exit channel pore.
source: First, the eIF3a (dark blue) NTD and eIF3c (light blue) CTD PCI (Proteasome/Cop9/eIF3) domains form a heterodimer that binds below the platform, near the mRNA exit channel pore (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: A second contact is formed closer to the mRNA entry-channel side of the PIC, in the vicinity of helix 16 (h16) and helix 18 (h18) of the 40S rRNA.
source: A second contact is formed closer to the mRNA entry-channel side of the PIC (Figure 1A), in the vicinity of helix 16 (h16) and helix 18 (h18) of the 40S rRNA.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: This contact is made by the eIF3b β-propeller domain.
source: This contact is made by the eIF3b (light blue) β-propeller domain, consistent with its described interaction with uS4 (Liu et al., 2014), and is likely connected to the first contact via a previously identified interaction between the eIF3b RRM and the eIF3a CTD (Valasek et al., 2001b; Valášek et al., 2002), which likely spans the solvent face (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: The eIF3b β-propeller domain interacts with uS4.
source: This contact is made by the eIF3b (light blue) β-propeller domain, consistent with its described interaction with uS4 (Liu et al., 2014), and is likely connected to the first contact via a previously identified interaction between the eIF3b RRM and the eIF3a CTD (Valasek et al., 2001b; Valášek et al., 2002), which likely spans the solvent face (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: The eIF3b RRM interacts with the eIF3a CTD.
source: This contact is made by the eIF3b (light blue) β-propeller domain, consistent with its described interaction with uS4 (Liu et al., 2014), and is likely connected to the first contact via a previously identified interaction between the eIF3b RRM and the eIF3a CTD (Valasek et al., 2001b; Valášek et al., 2002), which likely spans the solvent face (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Valasek et al., 2001b and Valášek et al., 2002.

claim: In both the mammalian structure and the yeast eIF3•40S•eIF1•eIF1A structure, the eIF3i and eIF3g subunits are found above the eIF3b subunit, near the solvent-face opening of the mRNA entry channel.
source: In both the mammalian structure and the yeast eIF3•40S•eIF1•eIF1A structure, the eIF3i and eIF3g subunits are found above the eIF3b subunit, near the solvent-face opening of the mRNA entry channel; with the exception of the non-essential eIF3j subunit, no density for eIF3 was observed on the intersubunit face of the 40S in these structures.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from cited studies.

claim: With the exception of the non-essential eIF3j subunit, no density for eIF3 was observed on the intersubunit face of the 40S in the mammalian structure and the yeast eIF3•40S•eIF1•eIF1A structure.
source: In both the mammalian structure and the yeast eIF3•40S•eIF1•eIF1A structure, the eIF3i and eIF3g subunits are found above the eIF3b subunit, near the solvent-face opening of the mRNA entry channel; with the exception of the non-essential eIF3j subunit, no density for eIF3 was observed on the intersubunit face of the 40S in these structures.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from cited studies.

claim: In the partial 48S structure, the eIF3c NTD extends from the eIF3a/eIF3c PCI heterodimer near the exit channel towards the intersubunit face, projecting near the P-site.
source: In the partial 48S structure (Figure 1B), the eIF3c (light blue) NTD extends from the eIF3a/eIF3c PCI heterodimer near the exit channel towards the intersubunit face, projecting near the P-site, where it appears to interact with eIF1 (pink).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The eIF3c NTD appears to interact with eIF1.
source: In the partial 48S structure (Figure 1B), the eIF3c (light blue) NTD extends from the eIF3a/eIF3c PCI heterodimer near the exit channel towards the intersubunit face, projecting near the P-site, where it appears to interact with eIF1 (pink).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Near the entry channel, the eIF3a CTD extends away from eIF3b, wrapping around the 40S, spanning the intersubunit face, and nearly meeting the eIF3c NTD near the P-site, effectively encircling the 43S PIC.
source: Near the entry channel, the eIF3a CTD extends away from eIF3b (Figure 1A), wrapping around the 40S, spanning the intersubunit face, and nearly meeting the eIF3c NTD near the P-site, effectively encircling the 43S PIC (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figures 1A and 1C.

claim: In the py48S-closed structure, the eIF3i and eIF3g subunits are located together with the eIF3b C-terminal region on the intersubunit face near the A site and below the intersubunit-face opening of the mRNA entry channel.
source: In this structure, the eIF3i (maroon) and eIF3g (red) subunits are located together with the eIF3b C-terminal region on the intersubunit face near the A site and below the intersubunit-face opening of the mRNA entry channel, where eIF3i interacts with the eIF2γ portion of the TC (green and charcoal).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In the py48S-closed structure, eIF3i interacts with the eIF2γ portion of the TC.
source: In this structure, the eIF3i (maroon) and eIF3g (red) subunits are located together with the eIF3b C-terminal region on the intersubunit face near the A site and below the intersubunit-face opening of the mRNA entry channel, where eIF3i interacts with the eIF2γ portion of the TC (green and charcoal).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In a recent structure of mammalian eIF3 bound to an apparently late-stage initiation complex, eIF3i was found at a distinct location on the intersubunit face of the PIC.
source: In a recent structure of mammalian eIF3 bound to an apparently late-stage initiation complex, eIF3i was found at a distinct location on the intersubunit face of the PIC, leading to the suggestion that the density observed near TC in the yeast py48S-closed structure is in fact the β-propeller of eIF3b and not eIF3i (Simonetti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simonetti et al., 2016.

claim: It has been suggested that the density observed near TC in the yeast py48S-closed structure is in fact the β-propeller of eIF3b and not eIF3i.
source: In a recent structure of mammalian eIF3 bound to an apparently late-stage initiation complex, eIF3i was found at a distinct location on the intersubunit face of the PIC, leading to the suggestion that the density observed near TC in the yeast py48S-closed structure is in fact the β-propeller of eIF3b and not eIF3i (Simonetti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simonetti et al., 2016.

claim: The eIF3a CTD interacts with the eIF3b RRM.
source: These studies established interactions between the eIF3a CTD and the eIF3b RRM Valasek et al., 2001b), the 40S latch components uS3/uS5 and h16/18 (Chiu et al., 2010; Valášek et al., 2003), and with TC at its extreme C-terminus (Valášek et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valasek et al., 2001b.

claim: The eIF3a CTD interacts with the 40S latch components uS3/uS5 and h16/18.
source: These studies established interactions between the eIF3a CTD and the eIF3b RRM Valasek et al., 2001b), the 40S latch components uS3/uS5 and h16/18 (Chiu et al., 2010; Valášek et al., 2003), and with TC at its extreme C-terminus (Valášek et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chiu et al., 2010 and Valášek et al., 2003.

claim: The eIF3a CTD interacts with TC at its extreme C-terminus.
source: These studies established interactions between the eIF3a CTD and the eIF3b RRM Valasek et al., 2001b), the 40S latch components uS3/uS5 and h16/18 (Chiu et al., 2010; Valášek et al., 2003), and with TC at its extreme C-terminus (Valášek et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valášek et al., 2002.

claim: The C-terminal region of eIF3b is required for binding of eIF3i and eIF3g.
source: The C-terminal region of eIF3b was previously shown to be required for binding of eIF3i and eIF3g (Asano et al., 1998; Herrmannová et al., 2012), the latter of which was observed to interact with uS3 and uS10 (Cuchalova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asano et al., 1998 and Herrmannová et al., 2012.

claim: eIF3g interacts with uS3 and uS10.

claim: The eIF3c NTD interacts with both eIF5 and eIF1.

claim: Mutations in the eIF3c NTD affect the fidelity of start-codon recognition.

claim: The eIF3i DDKK mutation disrupts the interaction between the eIF3i/g module and eIF3b, resulting in the dissociation of eIF3i/g from the sub-complex containing the a, b, and c subunits.

claim: eIF3 purified from DDKK cells yields the WT eIF3a/b/c sub-complex.

claim: The prt1-1 mutation is a point-substitution (S555F) within the eIF3b β-propeller domain.
source: The prt1-1 mutation was the first functional variant of eIF3 to be identified (Evans et al., 1995; Hartwell and McLaughlin, 1969) and is a point-substitution (S555F) within the eIF3b β-propeller domain that contacts the 40S subunit and is connected to the eIF3i/g module of the entry-channel arm via the C-terminal segment of eIF3b (Herrmannová et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The prt1-1 mutation was the first functional variant of eIF3 to be identified.
source: The prt1-1 mutation was the first functional variant of eIF3 to be identified (Evans et al., 1995; Hartwell and McLaughlin, 1969) and is a point-substitution (S555F) within the eIF3b β-propeller domain that contacts the 40S subunit and is connected to the eIF3i/g module of the entry-channel arm via the C-terminal segment of eIF3b (Herrmannová et al., 2012).

claim: The ∆8 mutation disrupts a previously identified interaction between eIF3a and uS2.

claim: The ∆8 mutation apparently weakens the eIF3:40S interaction.
source: The ∆8 mutation disrupts a previously identified interaction between eIF3a and uS2 (Valášek et al., 2003), apparently weakening the eIF3:40S interaction (Szamecz et al., 2008), whereas the Box37 substitution predominantly reduces mRNA association with native PICs in vivo (Khoshnevis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Szamecz et al., 2008.

claim: The Box37 substitution predominantly reduces mRNA association with native PICs in vivo.
source: The ∆8 mutation disrupts a previously identified interaction between eIF3a and uS2 (Valášek et al., 2003), apparently weakening the eIF3:40S interaction (Szamecz et al., 2008), whereas the Box37 substitution predominantly reduces mRNA association with native PICs in vivo (Khoshnevis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khoshnevis et al., 2014.

claim: The ∆60 mutation reduces the amount of both eIF3 and eIF5 in 43S PICS.

claim: The GAP85 and Box12-SPW mutations affect the amount of eIF1 bound to 43S PICs.

claim: The GAP85 and Box12-SPW mutations appear to interfere with stringent selection of the AUG start-codon.

claim: WT eIF3 binds tightly to the 43S complex, with a dissociation constant (KD) near or below 38 nM.

claim: Mutations in the entry channel arm of eIF3 weaken its binding by up to ~3 fold.

claim: The H725P mutation decreases the apparent affinity of eIF3 for the 43S PIC by ~2 fold.

claim: The R731I mutation decreases the apparent affinity of eIF3 for the 43S PIC by ~3 fold.

claim: The Box6 mutant does not affect the apparent affinity of eIF3 for the 43S complex.

source: The a/b/c sub-complex lacking the i and g subunits exhibits ~2 fold weaker apparent affinity for the 43S PIC than the WT factor, whereas the eIF3i Q258R and the eIF3g KLF mutations do not manifest any effect on the 43S:eIF3 interaction.

claim: The ∆8 truncation weakens the apparent 43S:eIF3 affinity by ~2 fold or less.

claim: The Box37 substitution weakens the apparent 43S:eIF3 affinity by ~2 fold or less.
source: We observe similarly modest effects in the case of the exit-channel mutants of the eIF3a NTD, the ∆8 truncation and Box37 substitution. Both weaken the apparent 43S:eIF3 affinity by ~2 fold or less.

claim: The ∆60 mutation within the eIF3c PCI domain does not affect the 43S:eIF3 affinity.

claim: The Box12-SPW mutation weakens the 43S:eIF3 interaction ~2 fold.

claim: The GAP85 mutation does not appear to affect the binding of eIF3 to 43S PICs.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: WT eIF3 binds 48S PICs tightly (KD ≤ 38 nM), similar to what was observed for 43S PICs lacking mRNA.
source: WT eIF3 binds 48S PICs tightly (KD ≤ 38 nM), similar to what we observed for 43S PICs lacking mRNA.

claim: In the absence of mRNA, the affinity of TC for the 43S PIC is 104 ± 15 nM.

claim: In the presence of AUG-containing model mRNA, the affinity of TC for the 43S PIC is ~10 pM.

claim: Reductions in TC recruitment endpoints may be due to a shift in the balance of complexes between two conformational states: one in which TC is stably bound and one in which it dissociates during gel electrophoresis.
source: Previous work has suggested that such reductions may be due to a shift in the balance of complexes between two conformational states: one in which TC is stably bound and one in which it dissociates during gel electrophoresis (Kapp et al., 2006; Kolitz et al., 2009).

claim: The conformational states related to TC binding may be related to the open and closed conformations of the PIC.
source: It is possible that these states are related to the open and closed conformations of the PIC and that eIF3 modulates their relative stabilities.

claim: Segments of eIF3b, the eIF3a CTD, and eIF3 i/g module contribute to stabilizing TC binding to the 43S PIC.

claim: In the presence of WT eIF3, mRNA recruitment occurs with an apparent rate constant of 0.27 ± 0.023 min−1.

claim: The Q258R mutation in eIF3i has little effect on the kinetics of RPL41A mRNA recruitment.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The prt1-1 mutation slows recruitment by approximately 4- to 5-fold.

claim: The rnp1 mutation slows recruitment by approximately 4- to 5-fold.

claim: The Box12-SPW mutation slows mRNA recruitment by ~2 fold.
source: The eIF3c NTD mutations GAP85and Box12-SPW, thought to be located on the opposite side of the PIC near the P site, also slow mRNA recruitment by ~2 fold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Mutations within the eIF3 exit channel arm only slightly reduce the rate of mRNA recruitment.
source: Mutations within the eIF3 exit channel arm, either in the eIF3a NTD (Δ8 and Box37) or the eIF3c CTD (Δ60) PCI domains, only slightly reduce the rate of mRNA recruitment; nonetheless, Box37 significantly slows recruitment at 37˚C (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), consistent with its temperature-sensitive phenotype in vivo (Khoshnevis et al., 2014).

claim: Box37 significantly slows recruitment at 37˚C, consistent with its temperature-sensitive phenotype in vivo.

claim: In the presence of eIF3, recruitment of mid-AUG mRNA occurs within 15 s, faster than the time resolution of the assay.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The maximal extent of recruitment of the mid-AUG mRNA is similar in both the presence and absence of eIF3.

claim: The absence of mRNA in the exit channel slightly destabilizes its binding to the 48S PIC.

evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: There is a moderate decrease in the extent of recruitment of 5'5-AUG mRNA in the absence of eIF3.

claim: eIF3 makes a moderate contribution to stable binding of mRNA in the entry channel.

claim: There is almost no recruitment of 3'5-AUG mRNA in the absence of eIF3.

claim: Stable binding of mRNA in the exit channel is fully dependent on eIF3.

evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The eIF3a CTD mutations H725P, R731I, and Box6 diminish recruitment of 5'5-AUG mRNA to essentially the same reduced level observed in the absence of eIF3.

evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The binding of 5'5-AUG mRNA is dramatically reduced in the presence of the a/b/c sub-complex lacking the i and g subunits, even as compared to the absence of eIF3.
source: Though the eIF3g KLF and eIF3i Q258R mutations do not destabilize the binding of the 5'5-AUG mRNA, its binding is dramatically reduced in the presence of the a/b/c sub-complex lacking the i and g subunits, even as compared to the absence of eIF3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The ∆8 truncation mimics the complete absence of eIF3 in its effect on recruitment of 3'5-AUG mRNA.
source: In contrast, recruitment of the 3'5-AUG mRNA, which produces a complex with an empty entry channel, is dramatically impaired by the ∆8 truncation. This mutation, which eliminates the first 200 amino acids of the eIF3a NTD PCI domain in the factor's exit-channel arm, mimics the complete absence of eIF3; we observe no recruitment of the 3'5-AUG mRNA in the presence of ∆8 eIF3 (Figure 5C), despite the fact that this mutant factor and TC are both fully bound to the PIC under these conditions (Figure 2C, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The ∆8 mutation implicates the eIF3a NTD in stabilizing mRNA binding at the exit channel of the 48S PIC.
source: Together with the absence of any effect of the ∆8 mutant on recruitment of the 5'5-AUG mRNA (Figure 5, compare ∆8 in B and C), this implicates this region of eIF3a in stabilizing mRNA binding at the exit channel of the 48S PIC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The addition of six extra nucleotides in the 5'11-AUG mRNA relative to 5'5-AUG mRNA fully or partially rescues the recruitment defects for all three eIF3 variants affected by mutations in the eIF3a CTD.
source: The addition of the six extra nucleotides in the 5'11-AUG mRNA relative to 5'5-AUG mRNA fully or partially rescues the recruitment defects for all of the three eIF3 variants affected by mutations in the eIF3a CTD, leading to recruitment extents nearly as high as those observed with the mid-AUG mRNA that fills the exit channel and extends beyond it (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The 5'11-AUG mRNA partially rescues the defects observed in the absence of eIF3 and with the a/b/c sub-complex.
source: The 5'11-AUG mRNA also partially rescues the defects we observed in the absence of eIF3 and with the a/b/c sub-complex (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of a 48S PIC containing eIF3 shows the −10 nucleotide of the mRNA emerging from the constriction between the 40S head and platform, approximately 15 Å from the position of the eIF3a NTD.
source: Consistent with this, the cryo-EM structure of a 48S PIC containing eIF3 shows the −10 nucleotide of the mRNA emerging from the constriction between the 40S head and platform, approximately 15 Å from the position of the eIF3a NTD (Figure 6B) (Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and citation to Llácer et al., 2015.

claim: The 3'11-AUG mRNA partially rescues recruitment in the presence of the ∆8 variant, to an endpoint of 28 ± 1% of total mRNA recruited.
source: The 3'11-AUG mRNA, which programs a recruited complex with 11 nucleotides in the entry channel, partially rescues recruitment in the presence of the ∆8 variant, to an endpoint of 28 ± 1% of total mRNA recruited, but is not sufficient to restore recruitment to the levels observed on the mid-AUG mRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Increasing the length of mRNA in the entry channel to 14 and 17 nucleotides progressively rescues the ∆8 defect, resulting in endpoints of approximately 85 ± 1% and 90 ± 0.3%, respectively.
source: Increasing the length of mRNA in the entry channel to 14 and 17 nucleotides progressively rescues the defect, resulting in endpoints of approximately 85 ± 1% and 90 ± 0.3%, respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Between 14 and 17 nucleotides of mRNA is sufficient to restore interactions in the entry channel.
source: These extents of recruitment approach those observed in the presence of the ∆8 variant for both the 5'5-AUG and mid-AUG mRNAs (Figure 5A–B), which both result in a fully-occupied entry channel, suggesting that between 14 and 17 nucleotides of mRNA is sufficient to restore interactions there.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The ∆8 mutation reduces the amount of mRNA associated with native 43S PICs for all the mRNAs tested, but has a greater defect relative to WT cells on mRNAs with longer 5'UTRs.
source: Consistent with our prediction, the ∆8 mutation reduces the amount of mRNA associated with native 43S PICs for all the mRNAs we tested, but has a greater defect relative to WT cells on mRNAs with longer 5'UTRs (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Regions throughout eIF3 collaborate to stabilize its binding to the 43S PIC and directly promote mRNA recruitment.
source: Our data indicate that while regions throughout eIF3 collaborate to stabilize its binding to the 43S PIC and directly promote mRNA recruitment, the mRNA entry- and exit-channel arms of eIF3 play distinct roles within the PIC.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: The eIF3 exit-channel arm is required to stabilize the binding of mRNA at the exit channel within the 48S PIC.
source: The eIF3 exit-channel arm — and in particular the eIF3a NTD — is required to stabilize the binding of mRNA at the exit channel within the 48S PIC (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The entry-channel arm helps to stabilize mRNA binding in the entry channel.
source: In contrast, the entry-channel arm helps to stabilize mRNA binding in the entry channel but also participates in stabilizing TC binding to the PIC and in accelerating mRNA recruitment (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The entry-channel arm participates in stabilizing TC binding to the PIC.
source: In contrast, the entry-channel arm helps to stabilize mRNA binding in the entry channel but also participates in stabilizing TC binding to the PIC and in accelerating mRNA recruitment (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The entry-channel arm participates in accelerating mRNA recruitment.
source: In contrast, the entry-channel arm helps to stabilize mRNA binding in the entry channel but also participates in stabilizing TC binding to the PIC and in accelerating mRNA recruitment (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data.
